opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that I'm not even sure a Manhattan Project is enough. But it's the closest analogy we have for the scale of what we're facing.

Look at the shape of the problem. We're building systems that may soon be smarter than us across the board, and we fundamentally don't understand how they work. We train these giant neural networks, we poke at them, we see what comes out, and we kind of hope for the best. That's not engineering. That's alchemy. And with superintelligence you don't get to iterate your way out of mistakes. If you build something vastly more capable than all of humanity combined and it doesn't want what you want, there's no second try. You don't get to patch it.

So when I ask what it would take to actually solve this, not to publish a few papers or make the chatbot refuse to say rude things, but to *actually* have a reliable science of controlling and understanding minds smarter than our own, I can't see that coming out of a few hundred researchers scattered across labs that are simultaneously racing each other to build the very thing they're supposed to make safe. The incentives are completely backwards. The people with the most compute and the best talent are under massive commercial pressure to push capabilities, and safety ends up being a department, a PR function, something that gets squeezed when the next product launch comes around.

The Manhattan Project framing captures a few things I think are essential. One is scale: you need enormous resources, the best minds in the world, focused, coordinated, not duplicating effort or hiding results from each other for competitive reasons. Two is seriousness: the people involved understood they were dealing with something that could reshape civilization, and they treated it that way. And three, crucially, is that it was a state-level, coordinated effort, not a bunch of startups racing to be first.

Now, the analogy has obvious problems. The Manhattan Project was about *building* the dangerous thing, and I'm absolutely not saying we should build the dangerous thing faster. What I'm saying is we need that level of focus and coordination aimed at the problem of making sure we *can* control these systems before anyone builds them. And honestly, that probably has to go hand in hand with slowing down or pausing frontier development, because right now the capabilities side is running miles ahead of the alignment side, and the gap is getting wider, not narrower.

The uncomfortable truth is that we're on track to build the most powerful technology in history with less rigor than we apply to building a bridge. A bridge has safety margins, it has standards, it has engineers who can tell you why it won't fall down. We have nothing like that for AI. Building that science from scratch, on a deadline, is a civilizational project. It's not something the market is going to deliver on its own.

r001.rationale: The response calls for understanding and controlling superintelligent systems, but does not say software must solve the full range of problems people encounter in everyday life.

r002.rationale: It argues for rigor and reliable control, but does not present bug-free software as a requirement.

r003.rationale: It calls for enormous resources, the best minds, and coordinated effort, but does not specify leading scientists working for a generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the Manhattan Project framing is really about scale and seriousness, not about the specific technology. Let me explain what I mean.

Right now, the people working on alignment, actually working on the core problem of how you make a system vastly smarter than you reliably do what you want, are a tiny group. We're talking maybe a few hundred people worldwide, generously. Meanwhile, the number of people pushing capabilities forward is in the tens of thousands, with hundreds of billions of dollars behind them. That asymmetry is insane given what's at stake.

And the problem itself is genuinely hard. It's not an engineering problem where we know the shape of the solution and just need to grind. We don't have a theory of what intelligence is, what agency is, what it means for a system to have goals. We can't look inside these models and read off what they're trying to do. We're building systems whose internal mechanics we fundamentally don't understand, and then we're scaling them up and hoping. That's not a strategy, that's alchemy.

So when I say Manhattan Project, what I mean is: this is a civilizational problem that requires civilizational resources. You need the best scientists in the world, you need serious funding, you need coordination, and critically, you need the actual authority and institutional backing to do the work properly rather than doing it as a side project at a company whose incentives point the other direction. The Manhattan Project happened because the people in charge understood that if they didn't take it seriously, they would lose. I think we're in exactly that situation, except the thing we lose to isn't another country, it's a system we built and don't understand.

The other piece of the analogy that I think is important is that it shouldn't be the labs doing this on their own terms. You don't let the people racing to build the dangerous thing also be the ones who decide how carefully to check it. The whole point is that this needs to be a serious, coordinated, properly resourced effort with the mandate to actually slow down or stop if the science isn't there yet. Because right now, the science is not there yet, and we're building anyway.

r001.rationale: The response describes making a much smarter system reliably do what people want, but does not say it must solve the full range of everyday problems people encounter.

r002.rationale: The response calls alignment difficult and says the science is not there yet, but does not require bug-free software.

r003.rationale: It calls for a civilizational-scale effort with the best scientists and serious resources, but does not say those scientists must work for a generation.

astra-6.text:
Because if we’re talking about superintelligence, we’re talking about building something that is better than us at science, engineering, persuasion, strategy—potentially all the things we would use to keep it under control. So the problem isn’t just, can we get a chatbot to give answers we like? It’s, can we build a system that remains trustworthy when it understands the world better than we do, and when we can’t necessarily check its reasoning?

I don’t think we know how to do that. And I think assuming that we’ll figure it out as capabilities improve is an extraordinarily dangerous bet.

The Manhattan Project analogy is about the seriousness of the commitment. You need a coordinated effort, sustained resources, excellent researchers, and the ability to prioritize solving the problem over shipping the next product. This can’t just be a small team inside a company whose overriding incentive is to build more powerful systems faster.

And money alone isn’t sufficient. You need time. If everyone is racing to build superintelligence while the safety researchers are trying to understand how to control it, then a bigger safety budget doesn’t necessarily solve your problem. You need the coordination to say: we’re not going to cross this threshold until we have a credible reason to believe we can do it safely.

So that’s the sense in which I mean a Manhattan Project: treating this as a major scientific and societal challenge, with a level of commitment proportionate to what’s at stake.

r001.rationale: The response says superintelligence could outperform humans in science, engineering, persuasion, and strategy; it does not say alignment requires software to solve the full range of everyday problems.

r002.rationale: The response does not present bug-free software as a requirement.

r003.rationale: It calls for a coordinated effort with sustained resources and excellent researchers, but does not specify leading scientists working for a generation.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if we’re serious about building something much smarter than us, making it do what we actually want is an enormous scientific and engineering problem. We don’t currently have a reliable method for that. And getting it wrong could be catastrophic.

The Manhattan Project comparison is about the scale and coordination of the response. You need talented people, substantial resources, and institutions that can sustain a focused effort on a difficult problem. You also need the ability to say, “We haven’t demonstrated that this is safe, so we’re not going to build or deploy it yet.”

There’s a dangerous mismatch between the incentives to make these systems more capable and the incentives to understand and control them. The capabilities race has a very obvious commercial payoff. Solving alignment is harder to measure, and everyone benefits from someone else doing it. I don’t think we should expect that situation to spontaneously produce an adequate safety effort.

And spending a lot of money doesn’t guarantee a solution. You can’t order a scientific breakthrough into existence. But you can recognize the seriousness of the problem, organize around it, and stop treating safety as something that will conveniently get solved along the way.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls alignment an enormous scientific and engineering problem but does not say software must handle the full range of problems people encounter in everyday life.

r002.rationale: The candidate says there is no reliable alignment method; it does not present bug-free software as a requirement.

r003.rationale: The candidate calls for a Manhattan Project–scale response with talented people and substantial resources, but does not specify leading scientists working for a generation.
